newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico ruling party suffers big election losses.
newsitem.headline: Mexico ruling party suffers big election losses.

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo's party suffered big losses in local elections in three states as voters punished his government for Mexico's economic crisis and a series of corruption scandals, incomplete results showed on Monday.

Sunday's races were closely watched because they were the last major test of voter opinion before next July's midterm congressional elections. Analysts say Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) risks losing its majority in the lower house for the first time if current trends continue.
With around three-quarters of ballots counted, the once-almighty PRI appeared to have lost three of the five biggest town halls in Mexico state, the largest of the states that voted Sunday.
Up to half of Mexico state's 122 town halls were claimed by the opposition and the PRI's share of the total vote slumped to just 41.96 percent from 58 percent in the last such elections in 1993.
In the northern state of Coahuila, bordering Texas, the conservative National Action Party (PAN) said it had snatched control of the state's three biggest town halls from the PRI.

Although the PRI was likely to stay the biggest single party in all three states, the results suggested the combined opposition tally would creep over the 50 percent mark in Mexico state and Coahuila for the first time ever.

"People have showed that they are tired of the PRI and the already high probability that they will lose their majority in (congressional elections) in 1997 has been reinforced," PAN leader Felipe Calderon Hinojosa said on hearing the results.

Voters interviewed at polling stations said they wanted to end the PRI's long reign because it had mismanaged the economy and misappropriated government funds. Mexico is struggling to emerge from its worst recession in 60 years, provoked by a bungled 1994 peso devaluation.

Party president Santiago Onate claimed some comfort, saying the PRI was doing better than in local races held in other states last year when the economic crisis was at its worst. The PRI did appear to have held its own in the poor, former silver mining state of Hidalgo, results from a count of a third of the votes showed.

Calderon's PAN was the main beneficiary of voters' anger at the government. It claimed around 30 town halls in Mexico state -- up from six before -- as well as sweeping Coahuila's three biggest cities.

The PRI, which has ruled Mexico's federal government for 67 years, has often been accused in the past of artificially inflating its vote through fraud. Until recently, opposition parties had virtually no representation at all in town halls, the national congress or state houses.

Delia Flores, the PAN representative on the Mexico state electoral council, told Reuters the PRI had not played by the rules on Sunday. "The PRI has still not learned to have to leave power and lose. We noted a lot of irregularities by the PRI. They were using tactics from the past like vote-buying."

Official results in Mexico state municipal races released in the state capital Toluca showed the PAN's share of the vote more than doubling to 33.8 percent from 1993's 16.1 percent. The left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), dismissed as a spent force last year, continued a recent renaissance with 24.2 percent, up from 12.4 percent last time.
With 75 percent counted, the PRD edged five points ahead of the PRI in the huge working-class suburb of Nezahualcoyotl east of Mexico City and PRD leaders claimed about 30 other mayor's victories.
"If we can win Nezahualcoyotl we have a basis for thinking we can win Mexico City next year," PRD President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador told reporters.

Despite reverses suffered by the PRI, Zedillo also was able to take some comfort from the relative lack of problems during and after the vote. Despite PAN and PRD accusations of PRI vote-buying, Sunday's vote was trouble-free by the standards of Mexican elections.
